newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy CPI hits 27-year low, rate cut awaited.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy CPI hits 27-year low, rate cut awaited.

text.p: Italian inflation hit a 27-year low in November, according to figures published on Thursday, fuelling hopes of a cut in interest rates before Christmas.
The national statistics office ISTAT said consumer price inflation last month was 2.6 percent year-on-year, down from three percent in October and six percent in November 1995.

Financial markets showed scant reaction as the data was in line with expectations, but dealers said the drop to levels not seen since June 1969 when the consumer price index was 2.5 percent meant an interest rate cut was now long overdue.
Monthly inflation rose 0.3 percent in November, against 0.1 percent in October and 0.6 percent in November 1995, ISTAT said.
Annual inflation has fallen steadily since February and the downward trend should mean Prime Minister Romano Prodi is on track to meet his goal of average 1996 inflation of 3.9 percent.
Prodi, whose centre-left government took office in May, hailed the data as proof inflation had "obeyed" his policies.
However, he issued a sharp appeal to banks to consolidate the economic benefits of tamer inflation by cutting the interest rates they charge to companies, particularly small businesses.
"The drop in inflation is not sufficient to guarantee the country economic recovery," Prodi said in a statement. "We have also got to act on the cost of money."

Prodi said bank lending rates ranged between eight percent and 18 percent. "The size of the margin is excessive and completely anomalous, not only compared with other countries, but also compared with the situation in the past," he said.
"It is therefore necessary that the whole range of bank interest rates should fall."
The Bank of Italy has pursued a tough policy against inflation, waiting 14 months until July before cutting the key discount rate which sets the trend for commercial rates.

Further progress on inflation prompted a surprise second cut in October to 7.5 percent from 8.25. Economists now expect the central bank to clip another half a percentage point off the rate by mid-December.
"The inflation was bang in line with expectations and showed that an interest rate cut is now long overdue," said one trader on the London International Financial Futures Exchange.

European Commissioner Mario Monti, in Rome to present a campaign to explain the European Union to its citizens, hailed the decline in Italian inflation as a "reward for the government's economic policy but also for the single market".
The 15-nation EU has striven to build a free market in goods, people and services and Monti said this had boosted competition, helped to lower inflation and increase employment.

A tight lid on price rises is a key criterion against which EU states will be judged for fitness to join a single currency in 1999. Prodi is determined Italy will be a founder member and has set the average inflation target for 1997 at 2.5 percent.

Prodi, who took the lira back into the Exchange Rate Mechanism two weeks ago, has drawn up a tough 1997 budget to slice 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit and levy a "Euro-tax" to help Italy make the grade.
Trades union leaders welcomed the fall in inflation but said they were worried that Italy was hurtling into recession. ($1=1,535 lire)
